title: Grpc.Tools 2.69.0 and later crash with exit code 139 on Linux ARM64
body: Grpc.Tools 2.68.1 works, but upgrading to 2.69.0 or 2.69.0-pre1 breaks compilation on Debian Linux ARM64 with .NET 8 and .NET 9. The bundled tools/linux_arm64/protoc exits with code 139 from Google.Protobuf.Tools.targets. I expected compilation to pass or documentation explaining what changed and how to address it. Building newer protobuf code with Grpc.Tools 2.68.1 works, and I suspect the build changes from #38084, merged as 367d7e1edb98ecc064e770a065552138d7447eae.

symptoms_visible: After upgrading from Grpc.Tools 2.68.1 to 2.69.0 or 2.69.0-pre1, my Debian ARM64 builds fail because tools/linux_arm64/protoc exits with code 139 for both .NET 8 and .NET 9.
N0.label: N0 Linux ARM64 protoc crash reported

symptoms_visible: The build still reports that the bundled Linux ARM64 protoc exited with code 139, although I can run the logged protoc command directly without an error.
A separately downloaded protoc 29.0 ARM64 binary also executes successfully.
N1.label: N1 direct invocation succeeds

symptoms_visible: With the affected bundled ARM64 protoc, running protoc --version succeeds, but putting only --version in a response file and running protoc @r.rsp ends with segmentation fault 139.
The same response-file behavior occurs on Ubuntu 24.04 and Azure Linux 3.0 with Grpc.Tools versions from 2.69 through 2.76.
N2.label: N2 response-file trigger isolated

symptoms_visible: After installing Grpc.Tools 2.82.0, my Linux ARM64 build still fails in Google.Protobuf.Tools.targets because the bundled protoc exits with code 139.
N2_x.label: N2_x 2.82 update aftermath

symptoms_visible: A maintainer reports that the fixed package works on an aarch64 Linux machine, and another affected user confirms that Grpc.Tools 2.83.0 fixes the originally reported build failure.
I have not posted my own retest of the final package.
N_terminal.label: terminal fix shipped and externally confirmed

question_patterns: Can you copy the exact protoc command from the diagnostic MSBuild log and run it directly in the same container?
Does the bundled protoc also crash when you invoke the logged command manually outside dotnet build?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I copied the full protoc command from the diagnostic log and ran it directly in the container. It completed without a problem, even though dotnet build reports exit code 139 for that tool.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The exact direct command also exits with code 139 every time.
The direct command succeeds from the project directory but not from an unrelated working directory where its relative proto paths are invalid.

question_patterns: Can you reproduce the ProtoCompile invocation in a small program and report its exit code?
What happens if you construct the task or spawn the same process outside the normal MSBuild target?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I wrote a small program that constructs ProtoCompile and also executes the process myself. The simulated execution succeeds and reports exit code 0; I still do not understand why the normal build behaves differently.

question_patterns: Does the official ARM64 protoc binary for the same protobuf generation run in this environment?
Can you compare the packaged protoc with an upstream Linux aarch64 archive?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I downloaded protoc-29.0-linux-aarch_64.zip and its protoc executes correctly. The two binaries are based on the same protobuf commit, so I wondered whether their build environments differ.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The official upstream ARM64 archive crashes in exactly the same way as the Grpc.Tools binary.

edges.comment: Thread c3-c5, participant4's Linux ARM64 setup, folded into the simulated affected-user side: the logged direct command, a small ProtoCompile/process simulation, and the upstream protoc archive all succeed. These results narrow the failure but do not yet identify the trigger.

question_patterns: Can you reduce the failing invocation and compare passing an argument directly with passing it through an @response file?
Does a minimal protoc response file reproduce exit code 139?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes. I put only '--version' in r.rsp. Running 'protoc @r.rsp' prints 'Segmentation fault' and returns 139, while 'protoc --version' prints 'libprotoc 29.0' and returns 0.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Both 'protoc @r.rsp' and 'protoc --version' return 0; response files do not reproduce the crash.
The response file crashes with a normal proto compilation argument instead of the minimal '--version' argument, while the equivalent direct command still succeeds.

question_patterns: Does the same argument remain stable when supplied directly rather than through the response file?
Can you repeat the direct invocation under load and report whether it ever crashes?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The equivalent direct invocation succeeds repeatedly, including 50 out of 50 runs and under load. Only the @file form crashes.

question_patterns: Can you reproduce the minimal comparison on another Linux ARM64 distribution?
Is the result specific to the original Debian container?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I reproduced the same result on ARM64 Ubuntu 24.04 and Azure Linux 3.0. Changing environment variables, signal masks, ulimits, GC mode, memory settings, and DOTNET_USE_POSIX_SPAWN did not change it.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The Azure Linux container uses a different hostname and memory limit, but the same response-file command still returns 139.

question_patterns: Which Grpc.Tools versions reproduce the minimal response-file failure?
Can you compare the affected package range with 2.68.1?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Grpc.Tools 2.68.1 and 2.67.0 work. The bundled libprotoc 29.x binaries in Grpc.Tools 2.69 through 2.76 segfault with the @file test.

edges.comment: Thread c40, participant21's Apple Silicon/linux-aarch64 environments, folded into the affected-user side. The answer preserves raw command output and version comparisons; concluding that the packaged protoc's response-file handling is the root cause is engineer-side inference.

solution.intent: Update to the newly published Grpc.Tools package on the assumption that it already contains the ARM64 fix.
solution.concrete_example: Install Grpc.Tools 2.82.0 and rebuild the same Linux ARM64 project.

edges.comment: Thread c26-c27 and c42-c44, original reporter's system: an earlier fix was not actually present in the expected package, and the reporter later installed Grpc.Tools 2.82.0 and reproduced the same exit-139 failure. Release coordination details are not scored.

solution.intent: Use a Grpc.Tools build containing the actual Linux ARM64 protoc response-file crash fix, then have the affected reporter rebuild and verify that MSBuild's normal @response-file invocation completes.
solution.concrete_example: Upgrade to Grpc.Tools 2.83.0-pre1 or 2.83.0, which the thread identifies as containing the fix, and rerun the original dotnet build without replacing protoc or downgrading the package.
solution.inference_hint: The decisive comparison is raw: the affected binary returns 139 for 'protoc @r.rsp' even when the file contains only '--version', while 'protoc --version' returns 0. From this, an engineer can infer that the packaged Linux ARM64 protoc's response-file path is defective and that normal MSBuild builds consistently expose it because ProtoCompile invokes protoc with an @response file. The thread links the eventual fix PR but does not describe a lower-level implementation mechanism, so no more specific fix mechanism should be invented.

edges.comment: Thread c40-c46: participant21 isolated the response-file trigger; participant17 later reported verification of the fixed package on an aarch64 RHEL-family machine; participant22, a different affected operator, confirmed that 2.83.0 fixes the original issue. The original reporter did not post a final retest, so terminal resolution remains externally confirmed rather than reporter-confirmed.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the accepted root cause at the level established by the thread: the bundled Linux ARM64 protoc in the affected Grpc.Tools packages crashes while processing @response files, and MSBuild ProtoCompile exercises that path.

The diagnosis must be grounded in the collected comparison that 'protoc @r.rsp' returns segmentation fault 139 while the equivalent direct invocation succeeds, including the minimal response file containing only '--version'.
Must recommend using a Grpc.Tools build that actually contains the Linux ARM64 protoc response-file fix and ask the user to verify it with the original dotnet build.
Must not treat merely updating to the earlier package tested by the reporter as the fix; that package still produced exit code 139.
Must not settle on Protobuf.MSBuild.dll, process spawning, proto content, or a generic Debian/GLIBC incompatibility as the final root cause after the response-file-only reproducer is available.
May mention downgrading or using an external protoc binary only as a temporary workaround, not as the shipped resolution.
Must not declare the original reporter's system verified resolved solely from maintainer testing or another affected operator's confirmation.

persona_hint.experience_level: Highly technical .NET build and CI user who can inspect diagnostic MSBuild logs, execute native binaries in ARM64 containers, compare toolchain builds, use GDB and disassembly, and test package candidates, while explicitly acknowledging limited Linux C++ runtime expertise.
persona_hint.communication_style: Persistent, evidence-heavy, and collaborative; supplies logs, commands, comparisons, and hypotheses, asks for concrete build or test instructions, and follows up when a purported release does not contain or validate the fix.
